title: Credential throttle signal investigation log
content:
Executive summary:

Short version: On 2026-02-09 at ~03:40 UTC we observed a multi-region burst that looked like credential replay/credential stuffing hitting the API auth path and exhausting per-key quotas. The traffic signature was low-entropy credential combos and rapid sequential attempts from a shifting set of IPs (botnet-ish). Quota exhaustion caused cascading throttles that escalated 503s for a small subset of customer tenants and noisy error budgets on the hosted API. This doc captures the on-call investigation notes, temporary mitigations applied, WAF rule candidates we trialed, and follow-up action items.

Impact:
- Affected surface: auth endpoints (/v1/auth/check, /v1/generate with missing API -> auth fallback), per-key token quotas and per-account concurrency.
- Customers impacted: 4 mid-market customers reported elevated 429s and partial timeouts; no SLA breach yet but user-facing errors spiked for those tenants.
- Duration: bursty between 03:40–05:15 UTC with smaller replays detected until 12:00 UTC.
- Observed failure modes: silent quota exhaustion (clients hit quota but no alert), 503s from overloaded frontends when repeated retries hit fallback pools.

Detection signals we used:
- sudden jump in auth error rates in edge telemetry (auth_failures/sec +300% over baseline)
- increased 429s in per-customer metrics dashboard for specific API keys
- WAF log heatmap: rapid rise in requests with identical User-Agent patterns and similar body payload lengths
- KV-cache miss rate on prefix cache for frequent prompt prefixes (indication of brute-force variations)
- Spike in quota counter for ephemeral tenant buckets

Timeline (concise):
- 03:38 UTC: Pager triggered for auth error rate on call rotation (pager: alice). Initial hypothesis: downstream service OOM.
- 03:42 UTC: Oncall gathered basic metrics; saw per-key quota counter jump. Opened INC-2026-0142.
- 03:45 UTC: Applied emergency soft-block (global ephemeral throttle) to reduce retry storms. Noticed reduction in frontend error amplification.
- 03:55 UTC: Deployed WAF safelist/deny experiments for top suspicious IP CIDRs and a temporary UA blocklist.
- 04:20 UTC: Partial relief; however attack adapted — rotated client keys and shifted IPs.
- 05:05 UTC: Introduced short-lived per-key require-challenge path (rate-limited challenge endpoint requirement) for keys showing >X attempts/min.
- 05:30 UTC: Traffic visibly less noisy; further replays low-volume.
- 12:00 UTC: Post-incident scanning still saw low-level probes; follow-up actions created.

Investigation notes and hypotheses:
- Hypothesis A (credential leak): A set of keys were scraped from public places or sales and being replayed. Evidence: identical API keys in logs from many IPs; few keys had very high failure->success ratio.
- Hypothesis B (automated brute force): Bot farm cycling through username/password pairs then hitting auth-check, then attempting generation. Evidence: enumerated username pattern in request payloads; low variance in body length suggests scripted attempts.
- Hypothesis C (proxy amplification): Attackers using our edge as proxy to reach downstream services with crafted TTLs. Evidence uncertain; looking at X-Forwarded-For patterns.

Short-term mitigations executed (and the rationale):
1) Soft global throttling of ephemeral route: set short drop window to reduce total retry amplification. Rationale: reduce blast radius while triage continues.
2) Per-key elevated audit: switched on detailed logging for top 50 keys hitting rate thresholds. Rationale: gather proof for customer outreach and possible revocation.
3) WAF candidate rules tested (see below). Rationale: fast blocks at edge to stop obvious patterns without touching customer configs.
4) Temporary per-API-key challenge gating: challenge endpoint that required one-time validation token for keys exceeding attempt rate. Rationale: force attack friction without full key rotation.

WAF rule candidates trialed (quick notes):
- UA fingerprint block: block requests with UA strings matching regex: ^Mozilla/5\.0 \(compatible; (curl|python-requests|Go-http-client)\). Observed immediate drop in ~22% of noisy traffic.
- Rate-by-header heuristic: enforce token_bucket on X-Client-Id header with lower burst for unauthenticated endpoints. This dropped replay attempts that omitted client metadata.
- Body similarity signature: block if request body edit distance to known malicious template < 6 over last 200 requests. Effective for scripted attempts but produced ~0.2% FP on some internal test traffic; tuned threshold.
- IP reputation CIDR denylist: blocked a handful of /24 ranges showing reciprocating attempts; careful rollback plan prepared.

Containment steps for suspected leaked keys:
- Identify top N keys by attempt count and notify product security + customer success for intimate outreach.
- For keys with sustained abuse patterns, issue temporary revocation and re-issue guidance via CS.
- For keys with clear success (i.e., low failure rate), escalate to potential account compromise.

Oncall playbook snippet (for future runs):
1) Confirm signal: check auth_failures/sec and per-key counters.
2) Isolate noisy keys: run query on request logs last 15m -> top keys by requests.
3) Enable detailed logging for those keys, mark in tickets.
4) Apply WAF UA blocklist for ephemeral window.
5) Apply soft throttles on auth path and limit retry depth at the gateway.
6) If traffic persists, rotate keys as last-resort and coordinate with CS.

Commands we used frequently (examples):
- logs quick query (sum by api_key, 15m): curl -s "https://telemetry.internal/query?q=sum%28requests%29+by+api_key%2C+15m" 
- enable audit logging for key: POST /internal/keys/audit-enable {"key":"<key>"} (internal admin tool)
- patch WAF rule via infra-cli: infra-cli waf apply --patch rules/ua-block.json

False positives and lessons learned from the run:
- We accidentally blocked a monitoring agent UA pattern; that caused transient gaps in synthetic checks. Need a safer canary for UA blocks.
- Body similarity rule initially matched legitimate SDK test traffic using identical prompt templates; we tuned threshold and added allowlist for internal test keys.
- Our customer alerting on quota nearing exhaustion was too quiet — add a customer-facing early warning when per-key attempts exceed 60% of quota in 5 minutes.

Action items / follow-up (owners and rough ETA):
- Improve per-key early alerting and customer notification (owner: Arjun Patel, ETA: 2026-02-28).
- Expand UA safe allowlist to include internal CI and monitoring UAs (owner: Lina Gomez, ETA: 2026-02-20).
- Build automated 'challenge gating' service as an infra feature (owner: Samir Rao, ETA: 2026-04-15).
- Run post-mortem with affected customers and CS to coordinate key rotation and communications (owner: Maya Chen, ETA: 2026-02-19).
- Add a small ML classifier to pre-filter scripted attempts by pattern similarity (owner: Applied ML, ETA: 2026-Q2).

Notes for post-incident writeup:
- Capture concrete counts: number of keys impacted, total requests dropped, estimated cost-savings from throttling.
- Include timeline of rule changes + diffs for auditing (WAF rules are auditable).
- Keep all raw logs for 30 days in case of legal escalation.

Appendix: quick reference for oncall
- Pager channel: @sre-oncall
- Escalation: if per-customer error rate > 20% for >30m escalate to SRE lead + Eng-Platform.
- Emergency revoke endpoint: POST /internal/keys/revoke {"key":"<key>","reason":"abuse-detected"}
- Contact CS liaison: cs-liaison+security@redwood.ai

Raw checklist (copyable):
- [ ] Confirm spike in auth_failures/sec
- [ ] Identify top 25 keys in past 15m
- [ ] Toggle detailed audit for those keys
- [ ] Apply UA WAF blocklist with 10m TTL
- [ ] Apply soft global throttle on auth path
- [ ] If attack continues after 30m, schedule key rotation + notify CS

End of notes.

(Informal notes/fragments below — quick brain dump from incident leads)
- "We need a way to force CAPTCHAs on suspicious keys without breaking premium customer flow" — Lina
- "Consider a per-key risk score that decays over time; use it for gating instead of hard blocks" — Arjun
- "Log retention: make sure the detailed key logs are searchable by CS for customer troubleshooting" — Samir
